title: Camino de Santiago : A Yoga & Reflections Retreat

teachers.name: Jenniferlyn Chiemingo
bio: Jenniferlyn is known affectionately by her students + friends as JL…and the words joy, love, and yoga surely describe her best!

Through yoga on the mat and in travel, JL’s goal is to provide her students with the opportunity to experience genuine joy, love, and connection (a.k.a. yoga). JL’s unique yoga teaching style is a creation all her own and an experience from which all can benefit. They are flowing, grounding, spiritual and inspiring. When you step away from one of her Vinyasa classes, you will feel more connected to yourself and the world around you. She provides loving support to newbies while continually challenging regular practitioners to find greater depths in their practice.

JL first experienced yoga in 2000 when she was looking for a way to escape the daily stress from her job as a TV news producer in northern California. That was when yoga started to change her life. Overcome by the power and benefits of yoga in her own life, JL decided to move her career from the newsroom to the yoga mat in 2002. With curiosity and ambition, she followed her dream and began her training at Kripalu Center for Yoga & Health with an emphasis in Integrative Yoga Therapy. JL continued her training with Shiva Rea, embracing Vinyasa yoga. Through Vinyasa, she learned the powerful energizing and cleansing benefits of linking breath with movement.

JL is listed E-RYT with Yoga Alliance and has taught for more than 22 years in Seattle and the Bay Area. After more than 15 years leading international yoga retreats she partnered with Yoga & Adventures Worldwide in 2021 to bring travelers on our bespoke yoga adventures and beyond. These intimate getaways have the potential to change your life if you are open to the possibility…

intro: For more than a thousand years, people have walked the Camino seeking perspective, gratitude, courage, or simply the experience of slowing down.
about_body: For more than a thousand years, people have walked across Galicia toward Santiago de Compostela. They came for all kinds of reasons — grief, gratitude, a decision they couldn’t make sitting still. What they had in common was the willingness to put one foot in front of the other and let the road do its work.

We walk the final stretch of the Camino Portugués: roughly 110 kilometers from Vigo to Santiago, over six days of walking. Eucalyptus forests and vineyards, tidal rivers and stone villages, old bridges, hórreos, the smell of rain on granite. Then the last long day, and the city at the end of it.

Days begin with movement — yoga on a terrace, a stretch by the water, meditation before the first kilometer. Each day closes with something restorative: gentle practice, journaling, a long dinner with the people you’ve walked beside. In between, there’s the trail. Some days we walk together and talk. One day we walk entirely in silence. Most days you’ll find your own pace, and perhaps be surprised by what shows up in it.

Your bags travel ahead of you. Each night there’s a real bed, a good meal, and more often than not a garden, a pool, or a thermal spring waiting for you to close the day. This is a pilgrimage with soft landings — the walking is honest, and so is the rest.
A pilgrimage is a walk with intention. That’s all it has ever needed to be.

The road doesn’t ask you to believe anything. It asks you to keep going. To carry only what you actually need. To accept the weather. To greet strangers walking in the same direction. To let the day be simple: wake, move, walk, eat, rest, repeat.
Ten days of that changes something. Not dramatically, not all at once. but you tend to notice it on the way home.
Some days we walk without speaking. No conversation, no headphones, no phone — just breath and footfall. It’s the part people are most nervous about, and the part they remember.
Other days the road is social. Conversations at walking pace, shoulder to shoulder, when nobody has to hold eye contact. Long lunches, wine in a village square, circles at the beginning and the end.

The practice here is practical and kind to a walking body: hips, hamstrings, feet, shoulders. Mornings are for warming up and waking up. Evenings are slower — restorative shapes, breath, long holds. Each day comes with a journaling prompt, and time to sit with it. Meditation is offered and always optional.

text: Part of the pleasure of this route is that no two nights look alike.
We stay in casas rurales with their own particular charm — family-run, unhurried, the kind of place where breakfast is whatever came out of the garden.
We stay in traditional Galician pazos, stone manor houses with walled gardens and centuries of weather on them.
And we finish in Compostela at a Relais & Châteaux hotel with a spa, for two nights of proper pampering at the end of the walk.
All stays are the most charming along this route. Each is unique, well appointed and comfortable with ensuite bathrooms.

items: Camino de Santiago :

travel_tips.heading: Arrival & airports
items: We begin in Vigo and finish in Santiago de Compostela — two different cities, so book into one and out of the other.
Vigo (VGO) is the closest airport to our starting hotel, around 20 minutes away.

Santiago (SCQ), Lisbon (LIS) and Porto (OPO) are well connected and often better value; from Porto, there are direct trains and buses to Vigo in around 2–2.5 hours. A private taxi ride could be arranged to simplify the process. Pricing will depend on how many in the ride. Inquire for more.
For the return, Santiago airport is about 15 minutes from our final hotel.
Arrive a day or three early if you can. Starting a walking week jet-lagged is a hard way to begin.

travel_tips.heading: Preparing your body
items: This is not a technical trail, but it is six days of consecutive walking. Come with some kilometers already in your legs.
In the months before, build up to walking 15–20 km comfortably, ideally on back-to-back days.
Break everything in properly. Nothing new on day one — not shoes, not socks, not a pack.
Trail runners or light hiking shoes both work well; heavy boots are usually not necessary for the Portuguese Way route.

travel_tips.heading: Packing
items: Your suitcase travels between hotels each day, so pack it however you like — you’ll only carry a small day pack on the trail.
In the day pack: water bottle, sun protection, hat, a rain layer, snacks, blister care, and your journal (part of our gift to you). We will send a full packing list prior to the retreat.
Layers. Galicia is green because Galicia rains — a proper waterproof jacket earns its place in both seasons.
Two pairs of walking shoes if you have them, and more socks than feels reasonable. A comfy pair of squishy slides or Birks for when you’re not on the trail are essential.
A swimsuit for the pools, thermal baths and spas along the way.
One nicer outfit for the farewell dinner in Santiago.

travel_tips.heading: Weather
items: April: green, fresh and changeable. Expect 54-66°F, wildflowers, and a decent chance of rain.
September: warmer and more settled, around 63–75°F, with the harvest underway and long evenings.
Either way, mornings are cool and afternoons can be warm. Layers do most of the work.

travel_tips.heading: Yoga & props
items: Mats and props are provided at the hotels where we practice.
If you prefer your own mat, bring a light travel mat such as a Liforme (save 20% here).
Practices are designed around a walking body — accessible, restorative and always optional.
Part of our gift to you at opening circle will be a journal and a pen.

travel_tips.heading: Food & dietary notes
items: Galician cooking is seafood-forward and exceptional: percebes, pulpo, oysters at Arcade, Padrón peppers, Albariño.
Vegetarian and vegan options can be arranged with advance notice.
Gluten-free and allergy-friendly meals are possible, though cross-contamination may occur.
If you have a serious allergy, bring two epi-pens and let our team know where they are.
Meals on your own can be eaten along the trail under the shade of a tree or in a cafe made for pilgrims; dinners are available at or close to the hotels.

Tap water throughout Galicia is safe to drink, and we recommend bringing a refillable water bottle to fill at the hotels each morning and along the Camino where you’ll also find public fountains — just look for those marked “agua potable” (drinking water) and avoid drinking from unmarked natural springs.

travel_tips.heading: Your credential
items: Every pilgrim carries a credential — a small folded passport stamped at hotels, cafés and churches along the way.
Because we walk more than the final 100 kilometres, you’re eligible to collect your certificate on arrival in Santiago.
Collect at least two stamps a day. It’s a small ritual, and it becomes one of the things you keep.

travel_tips.heading: Travel & Medical insurance
items: We strongly recommend purchasing travel and trip cancellation insurance as soon as you book, to protect your investment and give you peace of mind while traveling. Cover your retreat here. We require that you show proof of medical insurance in case you need to use it.

faqs.question: How fit do I need to be?
answer: You should be comfortable walking 20 km in a day and happy to do it several days in a row. The terrain is gentle — this is about endurance, not difficulty. If a day feels like too much, a taxi is always available and nobody will think anything of it.

faqs.question: Do I have to carry my luggage?
answer: No. Your suitcase is transferred hotel to hotel every morning. You walk with a day pack.

faqs.question: Is this a religious retreat?
answer: No. The Camino is a thousand-year-old pilgrimage route and we walk it with respect for that history, but our frame is contemplative rather than religious. You’re welcome to visit the cathedral, and equally welcome not to. Silence, walking, journaling and practice are the spine of the week.

faqs.question: Do I have to walk every day?
answer: No. Six of the ten days involve walking, and you can opt out of any of them — if you need, an Uber can take you ahead to the next hotel. Most people walk more than they expected to.

faqs.question: What is the day of silence actually like?
answer: After morning practice, we set out and let the trail get quiet. For about four hours, there’s no conversation, no phones, no headphones — just the rhythm of your footsteps, the landscape around you, and whatever comes up along the way. You can choose to walk entirely on your own, or move quietly alongside others, finding your own pace and space for the day. We come back together in the evening to break the silence during our practice and reflect on the experience. It may be the part of the retreat that feels most unfamiliar going in — and one of the parts you remember most.

faqs.question: Will I get the Compostela certificate?
answer: Yes, if you’d like it. We walk well over the 100 km required, and you’ll collect stamps in your credential along the way.

faqs.question: Can I come on my own?
answer: Most people do. Shared rooms are available if you’d like to be matched with another solo traveller, and private rooms if you’d rather have your own space.

faqs.question: What if it rains?
answer: It probably will, at some point. Galicia’s green comes from somewhere. Bring a good jacket and it becomes part of the story rather than a problem.
